entries.meaning: The cutting tool or weapon.
examples: Hand me the bread knife.
All the knives need sharpening.
He cut the rope with a pocket knife.
The man was carrying a knife.
Police recovered two knives at the scene.
You could cut the tension with a knife.
She went under the knife last Tuesday.
That remark was a knife in the back.

senses.head: The cutting implement
examples: Hand me the bread knife.
All the knives need sharpening.
He cut the rope with a pocket knife.

senses.head: A weapon
examples: The man was carrying a knife.
Police recovered two knives at the scene.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: You could cut the tension with a knife.
She went under the knife last Tuesday.
That remark was a knife in the back.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the knives are in the drawer
entries.contrast: ✗ knifes is wrong as a noun plural — but it is right as a verb: he knifes through the water. The silent k survives from Old English, where it was pronounced.

entries.meaning: A married woman, considered in relation to her spouse.
examples: His wife teaches at the community college.
Both wives kept their own last names.
She is the wife of a well-known journalist.
The couples brought their wives and husbands.
Two midwives were on duty that night.
That's an old wives' tale — there's no evidence for it.

senses.head: A married woman
examples: His wife teaches at the community college.
Both wives kept their own last names.
She is the wife of a well-known journalist.
The couples brought their wives and husbands.

senses.head: In compounds
body: Housewife and midwife follow the same plural. (в составе сложных слов)
examples: Two midwives were on duty that night.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: That's an old wives' tale — there's no evidence for it.

entries.agreement: plural verb — their wives are coming
entries.contrast: ✗ wifes is always wrong. The possessive singular is wife's and the possessive plural wives' — three forms that sound alike in speech and are constantly confused in writing.

entries.meaning: The condition of being alive; the period of someone's existence; a way of living.
examples: Doctors fought to save his life.
Three lives were lost in the fire.
There is no life on that moon.
She spent her whole life in the same town.
Their lives changed completely after the move.
He wanted a quieter life.
City life never suited them.
There was no life in the room at all.
Not on your life.
She's the life of the party.

senses.head: The state of being alive
examples: Doctors fought to save his life.

There is no life on that moon.

senses.head: The period of someone's existence
examples: She spent her whole life in the same town.
Their lives changed completely after the move.

senses.head: A way of living
examples: He wanted a quieter life.
City life never suited them.

senses.head: Energy, liveliness
examples: There was no life in the room at all.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: Not on your life.
She's the life of the party.

entries.countability: countable, and uncountable in the abstract
entries.agreement: plural verb — their lives were changed
entries.contrast: The plural noun lives /laɪvz/ and the verb lives /lɪvz/ (she lives here) are spelled identically and pronounced differently. Long /aɪ/ for the noun, short /ɪ/ for the verb.

entries.meaning: The flat green growth on a plant; also a sheet of paper or a hinged section of a table.
examples: A single leaf drifted onto the windshield.
The leaves turn red in early October.
We raked leaves all afternoon.
Several leaves had been torn from the notebook.
Add both leaves and the table seats ten.
I'm turning over a new leaf this year.
She took a leaf out of his book and asked for a raise.

senses.head: Part of a plant
examples: A single leaf drifted onto the windshield.
The leaves turn red in early October.
We raked leaves all afternoon.

senses.head: A sheet of paper in a book
examples: Several leaves had been torn from the notebook.

senses.head: A hinged or removable section of a table
examples: Add both leaves and the table seats ten.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: I'm turning over a new leaf this year.
She took a leaf out of his book and asked for a raise.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the leaves are turning
entries.contrast: The plural noun leaves and the verb leaves (she leaves at six) are identical in both spelling and sound. Only the syntax tells them apart. Leafs is correct only as a verb — he leafs through the magazine — and in the team name Maple Leafs.

entries.meaning: A shaped mass of bread, or of anything baked in that shape.
examples: Pick up a loaf of bread on your way home.
Two loaves were still in the oven.
She bakes four loaves every Sunday.
He made a meat loaf for dinner.
Both sugar loaves were wrapped in blue paper.
They loafed on the porch until it got dark.

senses.head: A shaped quantity of bread
body: Loaf is the standard counter for uncountable bread. (буханка)
examples: Pick up a loaf of bread on your way home.
Two loaves were still in the oven.
She bakes four loaves every Sunday.

senses.head: Other food in that shape
examples: He made a meat loaf for dinner.
Both sugar loaves were wrapped in blue paper.

senses.head: As a verb — to idle
examples: They loafed on the porch until it got dark.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the loaves are cooling
entries.contrast: ✗ loafs is wrong as a noun — but right as a verb meaning 'to idle': he loafs around all weekend.

entries.meaning: Someone who steals.
examples: A thief took the bicycle from the porch.
The thieves were arrested the next morning.
Police believe the same thief hit four houses.
Car thieves target this neighborhood.
There is honor among thieves, supposedly.
He came like a thief in the night.

senses.head: Someone who steals
examples: A thief took the bicycle from the porch.
The thieves were arrested the next morning.
Police believe the same thief hit four houses.
Car thieves target this neighborhood.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: There is honor among thieves, supposedly.
He came like a thief in the night.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the thieves were caught
entries.contrast: ✗ thiefs is wrong. Note the sharp contrast with chief → chiefs, which is regular despite rhyming perfectly.

entries.meaning: The wild canine.
examples: A wolf crossed the ridge at dusk.
Wolves were reintroduced to the park in 1995.
The pack's wolves travel enormous distances.
He's a wolf in the boardroom.
That's a wolf in sheep's clothing.
They were keeping the wolf from the door.
Don't cry wolf unless you mean it.
He wolfed down two sandwiches.

senses.head: The animal
examples: A wolf crossed the ridge at dusk.
Wolves were reintroduced to the park in 1995.
The pack's wolves travel enormous distances.

senses.head: A predatory or greedy person
examples: He's a wolf in the boardroom.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: That's a wolf in sheep's clothing.
They were keeping the wolf from the door.
Don't cry wolf unless you mean it.

body: As a verb — to eat fast. (жадно есть)
examples: He wolfed down two sandwiches.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the wolves are howling
entries.contrast: ✗ wolfs is wrong as a noun — but correct as a verb: he wolfs down his lunch.

entries.meaning: A flat board for holding objects; also a ledge of rock.
examples: Put the box on the top shelf.
All the shelves were empty by noon.
He built the shelves himself.
The continental shelf drops away sharply here.
The plan has been on the shelf for years.
Check the shelf life before you buy it.

senses.head: A board for storage
examples: Put the box on the top shelf.
All the shelves were empty by noon.
He built the shelves himself.

senses.head: A ledge of rock or ice
examples: The continental shelf drops away sharply here.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: The plan has been on the shelf for years.
Check the shelf life before you buy it.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the shelves are full
entries.contrast: ✗ shelfs is wrong as a noun — but right as a verb meaning 'to postpone': the studio shelfs the project. More commonly the verb appears as shelved.

entries.meaning: A young cow or other large mammal; also the back of the lower leg.
examples: The calf was born just before dawn.
Six calves were sold at auction.
Whale calves stay close to their mothers.
He pulled a calf muscle running.
My calves ache after that climb.

senses.head: A young animal
examples: The calf was born just before dawn.
Six calves were sold at auction.
Whale calves stay close to their mothers.

senses.head: The muscle at the back of the lower leg
examples: He pulled a calf muscle running.
My calves ache after that climb.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the calves were born in spring
entries.contrast: The l is silent, as in half, palm, and calm. Two unrelated meanings share the word and the plural: the young animal and the muscle at the back of the lower leg.

entries.meaning: One of two equal parts.
examples: Cut the apple in half.
Both halves of the class scored the same.
She gave me half of her sandwich.
They scored twice in the second half.
Neither team looked sharp in the opening halves.
He doesn't know the half of it.
Let's go halves on the check. (fixed plural)

senses.head: One of two equal parts
examples: Cut the apple in half.
Both halves of the class scored the same.
She gave me half of her sandwich.

senses.head: One of two periods in a game
examples: They scored twice in the second half.
Neither team looked sharp in the opening halves.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: He doesn't know the half of it.
Let's go halves on the check. (fixed plural)

entries.agreement: plural verb — both halves are equal
entries.contrast: ✗ halfs is wrong. The verb is halve /hæv/ with a voiced v even in the singular: halve the recipe.

entries.meaning: A person's essential being; the whole of what someone is.
examples: She's finally back to her old self.
Their public and private selves barely resemble each other.
He wasn't quite himself — a different self entirely.
We poured ourselves some coffee.
Help yourselves to the food.
They taught themselves to code.

senses.head: A person's essential nature
examples: She's finally back to her old self.
Their public and private selves barely resemble each other.
He wasn't quite himself — a different self entirely.

senses.head: In reflexive pronouns
examples: We poured ourselves some coffee.
Help yourselves to the food.
They taught themselves to code.

entries.agreement: plural verb — their better selves were on display
entries.contrast: Every reflexive pronoun inherits this plural: myself → ourselves, yourself → yourselves, himself/herself/itself → themselves. ✗ themselfs and ✗ ourselfs are always wrong.

entries.meaning: A bundle of grain stalks, or of papers.
examples: The sheaves were stacked in the field.
Each sheaf was tied with twine.
She dropped a sheaf of documents on the desk.
He arrived carrying sheaves of printouts.
A thick sheaf of letters sat unopened.

senses.head: A bundle of cut grain
examples: The sheaves were stacked in the field.
Each sheaf was tied with twine.

senses.head: A bundle of papers
examples: She dropped a sheaf of documents on the desk.
He arrived carrying sheaves of printouts.
A thick sheaf of letters sat unopened.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the sheaves were stacked
entries.contrast: ✗ sheafs is wrong. Compare the near-identical-looking chief → chiefs, which is regular.

entries.meaning: A small mythical humanlike creature.
examples: In the story, an elf guards the bridge.
The elves work through the night.

Tolkien's elves are tall and grave, not small.
Every mall has a Santa and two elves by December.

senses.head: The mythical creature
examples: In the story, an elf guards the bridge.

Tolkien's elves are tall and grave, not small.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the elves were busy
entries.contrast: ✗ elfs is wrong. The adjective is elfin or elvish.

entries.meaning: A mythical small humanlike being; in astronomy, a small dense star.
examples: Seven dwarfs live in the cottage.
The dwarves forged the blade underground.
The sun will become a white dwarf.
Red dwarfs are the most common stars in the galaxy.
The new tower dwarfs everything around it.

senses.head: In myth and fantasy
examples: Seven dwarfs live in the cottage.
The dwarves forged the blade underground.

senses.head: In astronomy
examples: The sun will become a white dwarf.
Red dwarfs are the most common stars in the galaxy.

senses.head: As a verb — to make something look small
examples: The new tower dwarfs everything around it.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the dwarves were mining
entries.variants: dwarfs (astronomy, and the traditional plural) · dwarves (fantasy fiction, after Tolkien)
entries.contrast: Both plurals are correct, and usage has split by topic. Astronomy says white dwarfs; fantasy says dwarves, a spelling Tolkien popularized. Referring to people, person of short stature is the neutral modern term.

entries.meaning: The horny foot of a horse, cow, or similar animal.
examples: The horse had a stone lodged in its hoof.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the hooves were trimmed
entries.variants: hooves is now much commoner in American English than hoofs

entries.meaning: A length of cloth worn around the neck or head.
examples: She wrapped a wool scarf around her neck.

senses.head: The garment
examples: She wrapped a wool scarf around her neck.
All the scarves were half price.
He lost another scarf on the train.
A silk scarf was folded on the chair.

senses.head: As a verb — to eat fast
examples: They scarfed down the pizza in four minutes.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the scarves are on sale
entries.variants: scarves is the usual plural; scarfs is the plural of the carpentry sense and of the verb
entries.contrast: As a verb scarf means to eat quickly, and it is regular: he scarfs down his food.

examples: The ship tied up at the north wharf.

senses.head: The dock structure
examples: The ship tied up at the north wharf.
All the wharves were rebuilt after the storm.

We walked the length of the wharf at sunset.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the wharves were rebuilt
entries.variants: American English accepts both; wharves is somewhat commoner

entries.meaning: The people who work for an organization; also a long stick, or the set of lines music is written on.
examples: The staff is meeting at nine. (the body as one unit)
The staff are divided about the proposal. (the individuals)
Both hospitals' staffs were consulted.
She joined the staff last March.
The shepherd leaned on his staff.
Barrels are built from curved staves.
Write the melody on the upper staves.

senses.head: Employees, collectively
examples: The staff is meeting at nine. (the body as one unit)
The staff are divided about the proposal. (the individuals)
Both hospitals' staffs were consulted.
She joined the staff last March.

senses.head: A long stick or rod
examples: The shepherd leaned on his staff.
Barrels are built from curved staves.

senses.head: The five lines of written music
examples: Write the melody on the upper staves.

entries.countability: countable, and treated as a group in the 'employees' sense
entries.agreement: either — the staff is (the body) / are (the individuals)
entries.pattern: regular in one sense, -ves with a vowel change in the other
entries.variants: staffs (personnel) · staves (walking sticks, barrel slats, musical staves)
entries.contrast: Two plurals for two senses, and the irregular one also changes its vowel: /æ/ → /eɪ/. Employees are staffs; wooden rods and musical staves are staves.

entries.meaning: A leader, or the head of an organization.
examples: The chief of police gave a statement.
Both fire chiefs attended the hearing.
She was promoted to chief of surgery.
Tribal chiefs signed the agreement.
Three chiefs of staff have held the post this year.

senses.head: A leader or head
examples: The chief of police gave a statement.
Both fire chiefs attended the hearing.
She was promoted to chief of surgery.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the chiefs were present
entries.contrast: ✗ chieves is the classic over-application of the -ves rule. Thief becomes thieves, but chief does not — the two rhyme perfectly and behave differently. There is no way to predict it; it must be memorized.

entries.meaning: The covering on top of a building.

senses.head: The top covering of a building
examples: The roof leaks whenever it rains hard.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: He hit the roof when he saw the bill.
We all live under the same roof.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the roofs were damaged
entries.variants: ✗ rooves is an old spelling now considered an error in American English
entries.contrast: Compare hoof → hooves, which rhymes and does take -ves. Roof does not. ✗ Rooves will be marked wrong.

entries.meaning: Something accepted as true; confidence that something is so.
examples: Her religious beliefs are private.

Their political beliefs have not changed in forty years.

The crowd was beyond belief.

senses.head: Something held to be true
examples: Her religious beliefs are private.
It is a widely held belief that the building is haunted.
Their political beliefs have not changed in forty years.

senses.head: Faith or confidence
examples: He acted out of belief in the cause.
She lost all belief in the process.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: The crowd was beyond belief.

entries.countability: countable, and uncountable in the sense 'faith'
entries.agreement: plural verb — her beliefs are firm
entries.contrast: ✗ believes is not the noun plural — it is the verb believe in the third person: he believes. The noun is beliefs with an /f/, the verb believes with a /v/. Compare thief → thieves, which does change.

entries.meaning: A small square of cloth for wiping the nose or face.
examples: He offered her a clean handkerchief.

Silk handkerchiefs were part of the uniform.

senses.head: The cloth square
examples: He offered her a clean handkerchief.
Three folded handkerchiefs lay in the drawer.
She kept a handkerchief in her sleeve.
Silk handkerchiefs were part of the uniform.
The magician pulled four handkerchiefs from his fist.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the handkerchiefs were folded
entries.variants: handkerchiefs is standard in American English; handkerchieves is dated
entries.contrast: The d is silent and the first syllable is hank-, not ✗ hand-. Both plurals appear in dictionaries, but write handkerchiefs.
